In probability theory, the '''tail dependence''' of a pair of [[random variable]]s is a measure of their comovements in the tails of the [[probability distribution|distributions]]. The concept is used in [[extreme value theory]]. Random variables that appear to exhibit no correlation can show tail dependence in extreme deviations. For instance, it is a stylized fact of stock returns that they commonly exhibit tail dependence.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hartmann|first1=Philip|last2=Straetmans|first2=Stefan T.M.|last3=De Vries|first3=Casper G.|title=Asset Market Linkages in Crisis Periods|journal=Review of Economics and Statistics|date=2004|volume=86|issue=1|pages=313–326|doi=10.1162/003465304323023831|url=http://repository.tue.nl/548705|hdl=10419/152505|s2cid=56001186 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Definition==

The '''lower tail dependence''' is defined as<ref>{{Citation
  | last1 = McNeil
  | first1 = Alexander J.
  | last2 = Frey
  | first2 = Rüdiger
  | last3 = Embrechts
  | first3 = Paul
  | title = Quantitative Risk Management. Concepts, Techniques and Tools
  | place = Princeton, NJ
  | publisher = Princeton University Press
  | series = Princeton Series in Finance
  | year = 2005
  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=f5J_OZPeq50C
  | isbn = 978-0-691-12255-7
  | mr = 2175089
  | zbl = 1089.91037}}</ref>

: <math> \lambda_\ell = \lim_{q\rightarrow 0^+} \operatorname{P}(X_2 \le F_2^{-1}(q) \mid X_1 \le F_1^{-1}(q)). </math>
where
<math>F^{-1}(q)= {\rm inf} \{x \in \mathbb{R}: F(x)\geq q\}</math>,
that is, the inverse of the [[cumulative probability distribution function]] for ''q''.

The '''upper tail dependence''' is defined analogously as

: <math> \lambda_u = \lim_{q\rightarrow 1^-} \operatorname{P}(X_2 > F_2^{-1}(q) \mid X_1 > F_1^{-1}(q)). </math>
